scope.start: 37b: the dilemma put to R. Chiyya bar Abba about a pot forgotten on the stove (38a opens mid-exchange)
scope.end: 38b: Rav Yosef on an egg roasted beside an urn, and Mar son of Ravina's proof, which continues on 39a

sections.title: A Pot Forgotten on the Stove: Penalty for Shogeg, Mezid, or Both?
sections.gist: R. Chiyya bar Abba's ruling on forgotten food, two readings of his words, a baraita that challenges one reading, the history of the decree, and reconciling R. Meir and R. Yehuda.

children.title: 'And the Halakha Is No Different': Lenient or Strict Reading?
children.gist: R. Chiyya bar Abba compares forgetting a pot to cooking on Shabbat. Rabba and Rav Yosef read his words leniently, Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak strictly.

bullets.text: The question put to R. Chiyya bar Abba: one forgot a pot on the stove before Shabbat and it cooked on Shabbat. May the food be eaten? He was silent.
The next day he taught publicly: one who cooks on Shabbat *be'shogeg* may eat the food, *be'mezid* may not, "and the *halakha* is no different."
Rabba and Rav Yosef: the cook performed an action, so *be'mezid* he is forbidden. One who left a pot performed no action, so he may eat even if he left it intentionally.

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak: no one would cook intentionally and then claim it was an accident. One who leaves a pot might leave it deliberately and say "I forgot." So the Sages penalized him even when he truly forgot.

children.title: Baraita: R. Meir vs. R. Yehuda on Food Fully Cooked or Not
children.gist: A baraita forbids forgotten food only when it was left intentionally. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains it as predating the decree, but Rabba and Rav Yosef's reading is left as a *kashya*.

bullets.text: Baraita: if a pot was left on the stove unwittingly the food may be eaten, if intentionally it may not. This applies to water or food not yet fully heated or cooked.
R. Meir: water or food that was already fully heated or cooked may be eaten either way.

R. Yehuda: fully heated water is permitted, since it is *mitztamek ve'ra lo*. Fully cooked food is forbidden, since it is *mitztamek ve'yafeh lo* and he may stoke the coals. Cabbage, beans and chopped meat improve; whatever deteriorates is permitted.
For Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak there is no difficulty: the baraita was taught before the decree, and his own ruling reflects the law after it.

For Rabba and Rav Yosef, whichever period the baraita comes from, it contradicts them. If it predates the decree, the intentional case is the problem; if it follows the decree, the unwitting case is. *Kashya*.

chart.caption: The baraita: a forgotten pot that finished cooking on Shabbat

children.title: The Decree: Too Many Who 'Forgot'
children.gist: Rav's tradition: forgetting was once treated like cooking unwittingly, until people who left pots on purpose started claiming they had forgotten.

bullets.text: Rav Yehuda bar Shmuel, in the name of R. Abba, in the name of Rav Kahana, in the name of Rav: at first, one who cooked unwittingly or forgot a pot could eat the food, and one who acted intentionally could not.
When those who left pots intentionally and said "we forgot" became many, the Sages penalized even those who genuinely forgot.

returns_to.note: Explains the decree referred to in reconciling the baraita

children.title: R. Meir and R. Yehuda Reconciled: Lekhatchilah vs. Bedi'eved, Swept vs. Unswept
children.gist: This baraita seems to contradict each tanna's position in the earlier Tosefta. The contradictions are resolved by distinguishing before and after the fact, and swept and unswept stoves.

bullets.text: The earlier Tosefta: R. Meir says even Beit Hillel forbid leaving food on the stove, while R. Yehuda says Beit Hillel permit it. Both statements seem to contradict this baraita.
R. Meir: the earlier statement forbids leaving food *lekhatchilah*; here he permits eating it *bedi'eved*.
R. Yehuda: he permits a stove that is *garuf ve'katum* (swept or covered with ashes) and forbids one that is not.

sections.title: One Who Left a Pot on Purpose: Penalized? R. Yosei in Tzippori
sections.gist: R. Yosei allowed hot water but forbade shriveled eggs. The Gemara reads this as a ruling for the future and shows that overcooked eggs improve.

bullets.text: The question: if someone knowingly left his pot on the fire in violation of the law, did the Sages forbid him to eat the food?
Shmuel bar Natan, in the name of R. Chanina: in Tzippori R. Yosei did not forbid water left on the stove, but he did forbid shriveled eggs.
Rejected as proof: he forbade leaving eggs on the fire the following Shabbat, not eating them on that Shabbat.
So shriveled eggs are *mitztamek ve'yafeh lo*? Yes. Rav Chama bar Chanina: he and Rebbi were guests together, were served eggs shriveled to the size of crab apples (*uzradin*), and ate many of them.

sections.title: Chazarah on Shabbat: In Hand, on the Ground, and Intent
sections.gist: Beit Hillel permit returning a pot even on Shabbat itself. The limits depend on whether the pot was put on the ground and whether he meant to return it, with R. Yirmeya's and Rav Ashi's questions left unresolved.

bullets.text: Rav Sheshet: according to Beit Hillel, the pot may be returned on Shabbat itself.
Rav Oshaya: on Shabbat they brought R. Chiyya the Great a kettle (*kumkemos*) of hot water from the lower floor, poured him a cup and put the kettle back on the stove, and he said nothing.
R. Zerika, in the name of R. Abba, in the name of R. Tadai: only while the pot is still in his hand. Once he puts it on the ground, it may not be returned.
R. Ami: R. Tadai acted on his own. R. Chiyya, in the name of R. Yochanan: even from the ground it may be returned.
Rav Dimi and Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda disagree on the same two positions, each in the name of R. Elazar.
Chizkiya in the name of Abaye, first version: "in the hand" is permitted only if he intended to return it. By implication, from the ground it is forbidden even with that intent.
Second version: "on the ground" is forbidden only without that intent. By implication, while it is in his hand it may be returned even without intent.
R. Yirmeya asks about a pot hung on a stick or placed on a bed; Rav Ashi asks about moving the contents from one urn to another. *Teiku*.

columns: On the ground, intended to return

sections.title: Oven, Kupach and Stove: Inside, Atop, or Leaning Against
sections.gist: The Mishnah ranks the three heat sources by how much heat they hold. The Gemara debates leaning a pot against them and defines what a *kupach* is.

children.title: Mishnah: Oven Always Forbidden; Kupach Depends on Its Fuel
children.gist: An oven is forbidden even when lit with straw. A *kupach* lit with straw is like a stove, and one lit with pomace or wood is like an oven.

bullets.text: An oven lit even with straw or rakings: no pot may be placed inside it or on top of it.
A *kupach* lit with straw or rakings is like a stove. A *kupach* lit with pomace or wood is like an oven.

children.title: Leaning a Pot Against an Oven: Rav Yosef vs. Abaye
children.gist: Rav Yosef permits leaning a pot against an oven. Abaye infers a prohibition from the Mishnah, Rav Adda bar Ahava deflects the inference, and a baraita supports Abaye.

bullets.text: Rav Yosef: "inside" and "atop" are meant literally, so leaning a pot against an oven is permitted.

Abaye: a *kupach* "like an oven" is forbidden. It cannot mean placing a pot atop an unswept one, since even an unswept stove forbids that. So it must mean leaning, and leaning against an oven is forbidden.
Rav Adda bar Ahava: the Mishnah is dealing with a *kupach* and oven that are *garuf ve'katum*, and forbids placing a pot atop them even so.

A baraita supports Abaye: an oven lit with straw may not have a pot leaned against it, much less placed atop or inside it. A *kupach* lit with straw may have a pot leaned against it but not placed on top.

children.title: What Is a Kupach? Intermediate Heat, One Opening
children.gist: Rav Ashi explains the *kupach*'s intermediate status by its heat. R. Yosei bar Chanina defines its shape, confirmed by the Mishnah's laws of purity.

bullets.text: Rav Acha son of Rava asks: why does a *kupach* depend on its fuel? Rav Ashi: it is hotter than a stove but cooler than an oven.
R. Yosei bar Chanina: a *kupach* has room for one pot; a stove is a double *kupach* with room for two.
A proof from the laws of purity (Abaye, or R. Yirmeya): a stove split lengthwise becomes pure, but one split widthwise remains impure as two small stoves. A *kupach* split either way is pure.

sections.title: Toldot Ha'chamah: Egg Beside an Urn, Sun-Heated Cloths and Sand, the Tiberias Pipe
sections.gist: The Mishnah on indirect heating: an egg by an urn, cloths and sand, and the Tiberias pipe. The Gemara begins by asking about an egg that was roasted.

bullets.text: Mishnah: one may not place an egg beside an urn so that it roasts, and may not wrap it in cloths (R. Yosei permits this) or bury it in sand or road dust heated by the sun.

The people of Tiberias ran a cold-water pipe (*silon*) through a hot spring. The Sages ruled: on Shabbat the water is forbidden for washing and for drinking; on Yom Tov it is forbidden for washing but permitted for drinking.
Gemara: what if one did roast the egg? Rav Yosef: he is liable to a *chatat*. Mar son of Ravina begins a proof from a Mishnah.

key_terms.sense: food that improves as it shrivels
key_terms.definition: Food that, once cooked, keeps improving as it shrinks with further heating. Its opposite, mitztamek ve'ra lo, deteriorates with further heating.
key_terms.on_this_daf: R. Yehuda forbids fully cooked food on these grounds, and R. Yosei treats shriveled eggs as food of this kind.

key_terms.sense: a stove swept or covered with ashes
key_terms.definition: A stove whose coals have been swept out or covered with ash, so that a person will not come to stoke them.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Used to reconcile R. Yehuda's two statements, and in Rav Adda bar Ahava's reading of the Mishnah on the oven and the kupach.

key_terms.definition: A small stove with a single opening, hotter than a regular stove and cooler than an oven.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Its law depends on its fuel: lit with straw it is like a stove, lit with wood like an oven.

key_terms.definition: The distinction between violating a law by mistake and violating it knowingly.
key_terms.on_this_daf: The decree against deceivers penalized even one who truly forgot a pot on the stove.

judgment_calls: Rav's history of the decree could be merged into s3; kept separate as a distinct step, with returns_to.
R. Yosei in Tzippori is a new question about a deliberate violator, so it was made its own top-level section rather than placed under s1.
coverage_notes: No shiur for this daf; the entire outline is built from the Gemara text.
The 37b.9 dilemma is covered here because it opens the exchange that continues on 38a; the previous essay's tail ends before it.
